domainSenses.biology: Sense organs and receptor cells detect light, sound, chemicals or touch. Species differ in what they pick up: bees see ultraviolet and echolocating bats hear echoes of their own calls. Plants and microbes sense with no nervous system.
domainSenses.cognition: The brain builds a percept from sensory input and from what the person expects. Combining senses such as sight and sound helps with ambiguous input. Illusions show the building.
domainSenses.technology: Sensors such as cameras, microphones and accelerometers measure physical quantities and output numbers. A sensor detects only what it was built to measure, and can pick up what people cannot, such as infrared.
domainSenses.AI and computation: Technical reading: a program maps sensor numbers to labels it was trained to give, such as a word or an object name. AI4K12 calls this extracting meaning from sensory signals. The labels are the trainers' categories.

newConcepts.label: Emergence
newConcepts.definition: A pattern of a whole system that arises from many parts reacting to local conditions and to one another. No part directs the whole or holds the whole pattern. Parts can be cells, animals, people or programs.
newConcepts.why: The comparative flagship note lists system and emergence as concepts no space defines. Dimension 3 needs a name for no-controller patterns that claims nothing about quality, as Collective Intelligence does, or about human thinking, as Distributed Cognition does.
newConcepts.excludes: It does not mean mysterious or unexplainable, and the outcome need not be good. A planned parade is directed and does not count. No controller in the system leaves room for rules, leaders or designers elsewhere.
basis: paper p.22-23 (cell, quorum sensing, La-Ola wave, brain, norms, machine-human culture)
technology and AI senses: own extension of the paper

domainSenses.biology: Bacterial quorum sensing, ant trails, honeybee nest-site choice and gene regulation in a cell. No molecule, cell or animal holds the whole outcome. Each part reacts to local signals and to others, and the pattern follows.
domainSenses.cognition: Brain activity comes from billions of neurons with no single place where a controlling self sits. People still tend to imagine a small inner controller, and students often explain such patterns by a controlling agent.
domainSenses.culture: A stadium wave, a traffic jam, a passing trend or a spreading norm. A few people cannot reliably start, steer or end it. Institutions can add control, which makes the case partly directed.
domainSenses.technology: Many networks pass messages through routers that each follow local rules, so no one machine controls the whole route. People still set the shared protocols and the rules.
domainSenses.AI and computation: Agent-based models give each agent a simple rule and show group patterns such as flocks. A neural network's output comes from many units and weights. Designers choose the units, the rules and the training.

conceptNotes.note: The paper sharpens the accepted entry. A pattern exists with no sender and becomes information only for a receiver able to use it. A bit count states how unlikely a message is among known options and ignores its meaning. Stations tag these points and add meaning. The definition stays.

The paper splits the accepted structure in two. A cue is read and was never sent. A signal exists because of its effect on a receiver. In the paper selection sets up both sides. Convention and design are this design's extension. Cue and Signal name the parts. The definition stays.

The entry: a stand-in works only for a user who treats it as one. The strategy applies this to the thought that DNA is a message needing a coder (p.10). DNA is a structure used by machinery that evolved to use it, and a sender is hard to specify (p.11).

Students link information with knowledge and truth (paper p.5-6). Knowledge needs a holder with grounds, so a cue, a signal or a stored trace is not yet knowledge. No station tags it. Teachers can use it to separate information, misinformation and what a group has checked.

The paper reads organism-level meaning through selection and warns against anthropomorphism for single cells (p.14). The Agency note already needs no intention in biology and gives software designer-set goals. Receivers in biology stations never choose. Sensing is the half of Agency that the new Perception entry covers.

Receiver competencies can be evolved, developed or learned (paper p.12). The strategy uses Learning for the within-lifetime case: a child learns which cue to trust, a program adjusts numbers. Selection explains the across-generations case. Stations ask which of these made the receiver able to read a pattern.

The paper cites Brinkmann et al. on machine intelligences and human cultures (p.23). The AI sense of Culture, a proposed extension, is the home for the machine-culture case in station 7. Its debate note applies: whether machines learn socially is open, and the station says so.

Feedback loops make an input's significance depend on context in a cell (paper p.22). Many emergent cases include a loop, and the Emergence entry does not require one. Negative feedback damps change and positive feedback amplifies it. Station 7 uses the AI sense, where outputs return as later input.

Collective Intelligence compares a group with its members and needs a measure of doing better. Emergence names patterns with no controller whether or not they are good. Stations use Collective Intelligence only when quality is compared, as in the jar-guess case. Bee nest choice fits both.

Distributed Cognition covers thinking spread over people and tools for a human task. Emergence covers patterns with no controller where no thinking task is involved, such as a stadium wave or quorum sensing. A computer network belongs here only when it serves a human thinking task, as the entry says.

stations.move: Children collect things that tell them something though nobody made them to: paw prints in mud, dark clouds, the smell of baking. They sort the cards, then add a few things made to tell, such as a stop sign and a wave. They say who can use each pattern: a dog, a child, a toy robot. Some will say clouds are for rain. Ask who made them to tell.
stations.example: Paw prints tell a child that an animal passed by. A drawn stop sign was made to tell drivers.
stations.representation: Two sorting mats of picture cards, with a 'who can use it?' sticker on each card.
stations.challenge: Notice that a pattern can tell something though nobody made it, and that who it tells depends on who can use it.
evidence: paper p.4-6 (infants detect regularities; no study of children's conceptions of information in biology)
design bet: no study of this sorting task found. S11 and S73 report purpose and want explanations for clouds and robots, so expect them

stations.move: Students compare what a bee, a dog, an insect-eating bat, a child and a camera can pick up in the same garden: colours, smells, echoes, heat. A table lists the pattern, the organ or sensor, and who can use it. They ask why a bee sees flower patterns that a child cannot, and try an illusion to see the brain fill in.
stations.example: Flowers carry ultraviolet patterns that a bee sees and a child does not. A thermal camera shows heat that eyes miss.
stations.representation: Table with one row per receiver: pattern picked up, organ or sensor, who can use it.
stations.challenge: Same surroundings, different receivers. Say what each can use and why, with a first selection story: bees that saw flower patterns found more nectar and raised more young. Mark what a camera does that a sense organ does not.

stations.move: Students set two things that are passed on side by side: eye colour from parent to child and the rules of a game taught to a new class. For each they ask who sends it, what reads it, what can change on the way and whether anyone meant to send it. They treat DNA as a structure that cell machinery uses and ask who its sender would be.
stations.example: Nobody means to send eye colour to a child. A classmate is told the rules of a playground game on purpose.
stations.representation: Two-column table with rows for holder, sender, what reads it, change on the way, and meant or unmeant.
stations.challenge: Add the question 'did anyone mean to send it?' to a passing-on comparison and see that the answer differs between the two columns.
evidence: design bet: no study of DNA as a structure at this band

stations.move: Students draw the paper's two causal maps for a forager. In the cue map, a smell leads to a response that selection shaped in the receiver only. In the signal map, sender trait and receiver response are shaped together. They write what each pattern means to the receiver as the response it triggers. They then add a second cue and see how two cues settle an unclear reading.
stations.example: Rotting-fruit smell is a cue for a fly and an alarm call is a signal. A person combines sight and sound, and a self-driving car combines camera and radar.
stations.representation: Two causal maps with arrows, a 'means to the receiver' box on each, and a note on what shaped each side.
stations.challenge: Say what shaped each side of each map (selection, learning, design) and what each pattern means to that receiver. For a fly, 'means' only names a response selection favoured. Show a case where a second cue changes the reading.
evidence: design bet: no study of cue and signal maps at 6-8. S37 reports one-way causal thinking and the signal map is a two-way loop. The forager case and the second cue are own extension of the paper

stations.move: Students find a hidden pick among 2, 4 and 8 equally likely options with yes-or-no questions and count the questions. They compare two messages of the same size, one trivial and one urgent, and a true and a false one. They list what the count includes and what it leaves out, and who must read the message for it to matter.
stations.example: One of 8 cards takes 3 yes-or-no questions. For a finch beak or an app feature nobody knows the odds, so the count does not apply directly.
stations.representation: A tally of questions per game, then a table of what a bit count includes and leaves out.
stations.challenge: Count uncertainty for equal options, then show that two messages with the same count can differ in meaning, in truth and in who can use them.
evidence: Sachsen Informatik Kl. 7 teaches binary numbers (topic text), so students meet the content at this age
design bet: no study of this age found in the evidence bank

stations.move: Students fill the paper's payoff table for an alarm-call game: states of the world, receiver acts and payoffs for both sides, and see which pairings pay. They add a mimic that copies a predator's eyes and see which pairing now pays the sender. They compare a rumour and a phishing email in a break table: who gains, who meant it, can the receiver check?
stations.example: In the table's made-up numbers an alarm call pays caller and listeners. Moth eyespots may scare birds by copying a predator's eyes. A phishing email copies a bank.
stations.representation: Payoff table for states, receiver acts and both payoffs, plus a break table: who gains, who meant it, can it be checked.
stations.challenge: Separate a false pattern shaped by selection, one made on purpose, one made by mistake and one made by noise, and say which a receiver can check.
evidence: design bet: no study of payoff tables at 6-8. S49 covers adults and S53 strategic play in children

stations.move: Students collect cases where a pattern of the whole appears with no one steering it: bacteria switching on a shared behaviour, a bee swarm choosing a nest, a stadium wave, routers passing messages, a feed trained on clicks. For each they draw who senses what, mark the missing controller and mark who set the rules. They change one local rule in a swarm simulation.
stations.example: Honeybee scouts compare nest sites and the swarm moves once enough scouts agree. No bee holds the plan.
stations.representation: Cue and signal arrows between many parts, with an empty box where a controller would sit.
stations.challenge: Explain a whole-system pattern with no controller in the map. Find a case where a designer sets the rules and still does not direct the outcome. Is a feed that learns from people a culture? Researchers disagree.

stations.move: Students wire a small network by hand: three cue cards in, two units that each fire when enough inputs agree, one output. They set the weights from examples, then compare it with a neuron and a trained network. They ask where meaning sits: in a unit, in the weights, or in what the output is used for.
stations.example: Units sum smell, colour and softness cues and fire for 'ripe'. A neuron also sums inputs and fires but is far more complex. A trained image network has millions of such units.
stations.representation: Hand-built network of cards and weights beside labelled drawings of a neuron and a layered network.
stations.challenge: Find no controller inside each system, then name who set the weights. Say how a unit differs from a neuron. Say where meaning sits and why; the question is open.
evidence: paper p.23-24 (Rosenbaum 2014 on the brain; p.24 calls neural networks an underexplored approach)
design bet: hand-built unit is untested at this band. S75 gives no ages

stations.move: Students pick one pathway, a hormone acting on a cell or DNA to protein. They first write each step as 'this changes that' with no sender-receiver words. They retell it with the words send, read, decode and code, and mark each use as holding, misleading or unclear, using three tests: direction, matching states, active against passive parts.
stations.example: Insulin binds to a cell's receptor and the cell takes up sugar. A ribosome is said to read a messenger RNA. Does anything read, or does one structure change another?
stations.representation: Causal chain of steps, then a table: metaphor word, holds or misleads, why.
stations.challenge: Keep the information words that track a causal role. Drop reader and coder talk where it implies an interpreter or a designer, and say what each dropped word hid.
evidence: design bet: evidence for naming where an analogy breaks is thin with school students

stations.move: Students fill one analogy map for four receivers: a bacterium, a bird hearing song, a reader of a news post and a trained classifier. Rows: the pattern, who sent it, what made the receiver able to use it, what it means to that receiver, whether a bit count applies. They name what shaped each receiver and which Selection sense, if any, fits. Break cells use the vocabulary notes.
stations.example: Selection shaped the bacterium. Selection and learning shaped the bird. Convention and learning shaped the reader. Training against a score shaped the classifier.
stations.representation: Four-column analogy map with a filled break column, built from the does-not-carry-over notes.
stations.challenge: Say, row by row, where sender, receiver and meaning stop meaning the same thing, and which case needs no sender at all. For the bacterium, say why 'means' is shorthand for a response selection favoured.
evidence: design bet: evidence covers two-case comparisons. Four receivers is a bet

crossLinks: Bio-Core carries Information and communication at standards level (NGSS, KMK): what is received, stored, copied, passed on and responded to in genes, cells, senses and between organisms. It has no agency or goals and does not relate structure to meaning. This space does, building on those descriptions.

Signal differs by space. Bio-Core uses it for signal transduction and communication signals, as KMK does. Here a signal is a trait produced for its effect on a receiver. Station 9 tests the words send, read, decode and code on a pathway that KMK calls signal transduction.

Social-Core and Computational-Core keep their own terms: goals, rules and messages among people; data, state and programs. Stations 5, 6 and 10 state the break each way. A bit count ignores meaning, a rumour is judged by who gains and who meant it, and a program labels input without understanding.

Tool stations carry the forms. The paper's cue and signal causal maps are station 4 and its payoff tables for alarm calls and eyespots are station 6. Station 10 is an analogy map with a break column. Station 8 shares a stage with Tinbergen's bird song and feed case.

Station 7 links to Bridge Case B6 (Machine Culture and AI) via its feed case. The I2:9-12 indicator asks what stays the same and what differs. Stations 8 and 10 carry the 'what differs' half. Bridge Case B1 can reuse cue and signal. The I4 strand carries evolution from 3-5.

NetLogo collection: BeeSmart Hive Finding (waggle dances, quorum, no coordinator) and Swarming (emergence, no strand yet) can run in station 7. Evolution of Resource Use Through Behavior Imitation shows norms emerging from imitation bias. This design writes no NetLogo strand.

The Sachsen sample has no Verweis between the Biologie information topics (Kl. 5, 8, 10), Informatik Kl. 7 and the media topics of Ethik and Sachunterricht. Stations name several of them. The reading card (pattern, receiver, what shaped it, what it means, who sent it) gives teachers shared questions.

TheoryBase holds the cross-domain construct OE-CROSSDOMAINCONSTRUCT-information-processing-domain-general and a design principle asking for cross-references across subjects (OE-DESIGNPRINCIPLE-domain-general-competencies-cross-referenced). ConceptBase holds the earlier Information entry. New concepts should link to them on registration. Found by search only, records not opened.

Left unlinked: the I3:3-5 guess-my-rule stage has an AI4K12 link but no information station, because it tests rules and has no receiver question. AI4K12 consciousness items (4-D-i) stay with the Agency stages. Emotion reading (4-C-i) has no station.
gaps: No classroom study of the three-dimension framework exists, and the authors found no study of students' conceptions of information in biology (paper p.6). Every station is a proposal to test.

The evidence bank covers component skills such as analogy, causal maps, payoff games and systems thinking. It holds no study of information. Most stations rest on design bets, and each station's evidence field names the thin ones.
Dimension 3 has stations only at 9-12. A 6-8 precursor such as a class wave or an ant-trail model is left out because systems-thinking evidence for younger students is thin (S37, S40, S41).

AI4K12 items on digital encoding at 9-12 (1-A-iii) and on feature extraction and abstraction pipelines (1-B-ii to 1-B-iv) have no station. They belong to Computational-Core. A neural-network precursor at 3-5 or 6-8 is not placed, because no stage there could host it without adding a topic.
The stage concept lists still carry the old concepts. Cue, Signal, Meaning, Misinformation, Perception and Emergence appear in stations only until a person tags the stages.
The Sachsen sample has no information topic for Kl. 1-2, so station 1 has no Sachsen anchor, and station 3 runs ahead of Genetik in Kl. 10.

Not built: a station that maps the stimulus-response model taught in Sachsen Biologie Kl. 8 (Reflexbogen) to the cue and receiver model (paper p.14, 19), a joint Biologie, Informatik and Ethik lesson (paper p.25), a station on Knowledge and truth (paper p.5-6), and any evolution work at K-2.
reviewNotes: Everything here is AI-drafted and no subject expert has reviewed it. A reviewer has checked the draft once and the changes are merged in.

Check first: Meaning as a selection-shaped coupling (teleosemantics, Potter and Mitchell) is one philosophical account. The paper presents it as one account, uses goal language with a warning (p.13-15), and cites Kattmann (p.8-9) and Levy (p.18) against it. The Meaning entry, the boundary and stations 4, 8, 9 and 10 need a philosopher of biology or a biology educator.

Unverified: Maynard Smith and Harper (2003), Macdonald and Papineau (2006), Johnson (2011) and the journal version of Brinkmann et al. (2023) were not read here. Claims about them come from the paper's text or the evidence bank.
Levy is cited in the paper as 2010. The LiteratureBase record is OE-LITERATURE-levy-2011 (Information in Biology: A Fictionalist Account).

The TheoryBase construct was revised in a pull request (version 2.0.0) to withdraw the claim that Shannon's definition applies identically across systems. Until that merges, the accepted text still says so. This strategy does not repeat that reading. Reconcile before registering the new concepts.

Bit counts need known odds. The analogy map in the last 9-12 station has a row asking whether a bit count applies to each receiver, so students see that nobody knows the odds for a bacterium or a bird.

Hormones inside a body are listed as signals in some accounts. Levy (p.18-19) treats such talk as a useful fiction, and station 9 questions it. The Signal entry says what set producer and receiver up differs by domain.
Stations 7 and 8 were reworded after review, because routers, a feed and student-set weights all have rule-setters. The station tasks now ask where control sits.

Station 6 is the heaviest at 6-8: a payoff table, a mimic table and a rumour table. If the load is too high, drop the mimic table or the rumour table first. The 6-8 bit-counting game (station 5) and the hand-built network (station 8) have no age evidence in the bank. Test whether students can run them and whether they separate bits from meaning.
